lesson.title: The Full Burden on the Source: Apparent Power
lesson.summary: Apparent power measures the total volt-amperes a source must supply, combining real and reactive power through a right-triangle relationship called the power triangle.
lesson.body:
A source supplying an AC load has to be sized for the total current it delivers, not just for the fraction of that current that produces useful, average power. Apparent power, S, measures this total demand: it is simply the product of rms voltage and rms current, S = Vrms Irms, with no cos θ or sin θ factor at all, measured in volt-amperes, VA, rather than watts or VAR, to keep it distinct from both real and reactive power.

Because average power and reactive power are, in effect, perpendicular components of apparent power, one scaled by cos θ, the other by sin θ, and cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 for any angle, the three quantities relate through a right triangle known as the power triangle: S² = P² + Q². This is not a coincidence of algebra; it follows directly from S = Vrms Irms, P = Vrms Irms cos θ, and Q = Vrms Irms sin θ, since P² + Q² = (Vrms Irms)²(cos²θ + sin²θ) = (Vrms Irms)² = S².

For the series RL circuit, Vrms = 120 V and Irms = 2.4 A, so apparent power is S = 120 × 2.4 = 288 VA. Checking against the power triangle using the previously computed P = 172.8 W and Q = 230.4 VAR: P² + Q² = 172.8² + 230.4² = 29,859.84 + 53,084.16 = 82,944.0, and √82,944.0 = 288.0, which matches S exactly, confirming both the individual calculations and the underlying identity.

The gap between S and P is the practical reason apparent power matters to anyone who designs or pays for electrical equipment: a transformer, breaker, or generator must be rated for the full 288 VA of apparent power in this example, since that is the actual current, 2.4 A, flowing through its windings and conductors, even though only 172.8 W of that capacity is ever converted into useful work. A source forced to supply 288 VA to deliver 172.8 W of real power is working at less than its full potential from the customer's point of view, exactly the inefficiency that power factor, examined next, quantifies in a single number.

Apparent power also has a direct check using the impedance magnitude: S = Irms² |Z|. For the series RL circuit, Irms = 2.4 A and |Z| = 50 Ω, so S = (2.4)² × 50 = 5.76 × 50 = 288 VA exactly, matching the Vrms Irms calculation performed above. This is the very same relationship already seen in the impedance triangle, |Z|² = R² + X², simply scaled by Irms² on every term: S² = (Irms²|Z|)² = Irms⁴(R² + X²) = (Irms²R)² + (Irms²X)² = P² + Q², tying the power triangle directly back to the impedance triangle first introduced in the complex impedance section. This is also why utilities size distribution equipment, transformers, breakers, conductors, in kVA rather than kW: apparent power, not real power, determines how much current actually flows through that equipment and how hot its windings and conductors run, regardless of how much of that current ultimately does useful work at the load.
